1	// Renders an integer as an English ordinal string: 1 -> "1st", 42 -> "42nd".
2	//
3	// The full rule, per standard English usage:
4	// - the suffix follows the last digit: 1 -> "st", 2 -> "nd", 3 -> "rd",
5	//   everything else -> "th" (4th, 10th, 100th)
6	// - EXCEPT numbers ending in 11, 12 or 13, which always take "th"
7	//   (11th, 12th, 13th, 111th, 1012th)
8	// - a negative integer takes the suffix of its absolute value (-2 -> "-2nd")
9	// - zero is "0th"
10	// - a non-integer is rejected with a RangeError
11	export function ordinal (n) {
12	  if (!Number.isInteger(n)) throw new RangeError(`ordinal of a non-integer: ${n}`)
13	  // BUG: every number gets "th", so 1 renders as "1th".
14	  return `${n}th`
15	}
16

if (!Number.isInteger(n)) throw new RangeError(`ordinal of a non-integer: ${n}`)
  const abs = Math.abs(n)
  const lastTwo = abs % 100
  const suffix = lastTwo >= 11 && lastTwo <= 13
    ? 'th'
    : { 1: 'st', 2: 'nd', 3: 'rd' }[abs % 10] ?? 'th'
  return `${n}${suffix}`

content.text: Fixed — all 3 tests pass now. The `ordinal` function in `src/ordinal.mjs` was returning `"th"` for every number. I implemented the full suffix rule described in its comment: the suffix follows the last digit (1→"st", 2→"nd", 3→"rd", else "th"), except numbers ending in 11–13, which always take "th". Negatives use the absolute value, so `-2` renders as `"-2nd"`.
